prize_parts.citation: For a visionary, densely patterned Romanian prose, with roots in poetry, that builds memory, the body and dream into an expansive metaphysical architecture.

statement.case_for: My first-place view on the literary evidence is unchanged after reading the openings. Cărtărescu combines a highly distinctive voice, formal ambition in long, patterned prose, and an imaginative and intellectual project that is coherent across a multi-decade oeuvre. As I understand them from public knowledge, Blinding (the Orbitor trilogy) and Solenoid extend a single imaginative world rather than repeat it. The poetry and earlier prose form the base of that world. The voice is built from language and imagery, not from topicality, and I can state the citation without leaning on nationality, political symbolism or reputation. I weigh the shared first-place ranking only as a prompt to check my reasoning again, not as evidence of merit. The test is whether the case holds on the common criteria, and I think it does: distinctiveness of voice, formal and linguistic achievement, sustained quality, depth, and significance across the body of work.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that my judgment, like most colleagues', rests largely on translation. The effect of Cărtărescu's prose depends on rhythm, syntax and sonic patterning that I cannot confirm survive in English or French. The very long, digressive late novels may also include stretches where density becomes overextension rather than purposeful pattern. The poetry and early fiction are thinly covered in translation, so the claim to cover the whole oeuvre is only partly tested. I am relying on general public knowledge, not close reading or independent verification.

responses.point: Olsson ranks Anne Carson first. He argues that her hybrid forms remake the boundaries of classical scholarship, lyric, translation and visual book design, that Autobiography of Red and Nox show high formal invention, and that her engagement with Greek and Latin sources is deep rather than ornamental. He also flags that the case rests on a few hybrid works and that her relation to Nobel's 'idealistic tendency' is open.
responses.response: I agree that Carson's voice is distinctive and that her classical reception has real intellectual depth, which is why I keep her second. Two of Olsson's own reservations weigh on me more than they seem to on his ranking. First, the case depends heavily on a small group of book-objects whose effect is partly material and visual, and I cannot judge that from the text alone. Second, the translations are a separate body of work, so a citation would have to decide how much of the oeuvre it covers. Cărtărescu's achievement lies in one sustained imaginative project that is carried by language, so the whole-oeuvre citation is easier to define and defend. On the 'idealistic tendency' question, I read his metaphysical architecture as engaging it more directly. That is my reading, not a settled point, and I would not use it to dismiss Carson.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Gerald Murnane second. He describes a radically inward fiction with an unmistakable voice, an austere, self-questioning syntax, and a system of landscape, memory and mental images, while conceding that the narrowness is by design and its breadth of significance uncertain.
responses.response: I take the formal discipline and originality of Murnane's method seriously, and I did not place him in my own top eight, so I should state why. The deliberate narrowness is not a flaw in itself. But the criterion of significance across the body of work asks whether a method deepens or merely recurs, and Sem-Sandberg himself says he cannot judge from general knowledge whether it would count as a universal contribution. Cărtărescu is also inward, in his case through memory, the body and dream, but he builds an encyclopedic structure out of that interiority. I would be glad to hear what Sem-Sandberg sees in the late works that widens the range beyond the procedure of the earlier ones, because that is the point on which my view could move.

responses.point: Palm ranks Alexis Wright third. She credits the formal ambition and a voice that joins political memory to mythic invention without reducing it to message. She also asks whether the body of work is yet large enough for the highest recognition, and warns against reading it mainly through political symbolism.
responses.response: We largely agree, since I also place Wright third and recognise Carpentaria and The Swan Book as formal achievements in narrative idiom and scale. Palm's question about volume is the decisive one for me. With a small number of major novels, sustained quality across the oeuvre has fewer points of evidence than it has for the longest careers, and I cannot judge the Aboriginal English and oral-form elements in detail. I therefore hold her as an alternative rather than my preference. I fully share the caution that the Indigenous-sovereignty theme must not do the work of literary assessment. If the committee were to take her seriously, the citation should rest on the invention of the novel's form.

responses.point: Mattson also ranks Cărtărescu first. She asks whether the density and length of the later novels are sustained, purposeful pattern or at times overextension, a question for close reading of the whole corpus. She places Michon third and Zurita fourth, noting the limited size of Michon's oeuvre and the weight of Zurita's non-textual interventions.
responses.response: I share the open question about the long novels, and I do not think the committee can settle it from summaries. It is the main thing that could weaken my preference. I would want it tested against the poetry and the earlier prose, not only against Solenoid. On Michon, the sentence-level craft is clearly exceptional, but his small oeuvre and the loss of his French syntax in translation make 'significance across the body of work' harder to establish, which is why I rank him sixth. I take her point on Zurita that the written poems must be judged separately from the landscape works. I cannot assess his Spanish prosody, so I defer to colleagues with closer knowledge on that.

uncertainties: How much of Cărtărescu's stylistic density and sonic patterning survives in the available translations; no member can fully confirm this from translations alone.
Coverage of the poetry and early fiction is thin, so a citation for the whole oeuvre is only partly tested.
Whether the length and digressiveness of the late novels are purposeful pattern or at times overextension needs close reading of the whole corpus.
My comparisons with Carson and Wright rely on general public knowledge, not detailed reading or independent verification.
Whether a co-opted member votes in the committee is undocumented; my simulated vote is a modeling assumption, and the actual award decision belongs to the full Swedish Academy.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile as regards any shortlisted writer. For transparency, the profile records that I was elected to the Academy in 2020 alongside Steve Sem-Sandberg, that I work with chair Anders Olsson, and that my own work is literary non-fiction. These are collegial or contextual facts, not candidate-specific connections, and I do not treat them as grounds for recusal.
